title: io, bufio & Readers/Writers
summary: Go models all streaming I/O with two tiny interfaces: `io.Reader` (`Read([]byte) (int, error)`) and `io.Writer` (`Write([]byte) (int, error)`). Because files, sockets, buffers, and HTTP bodies all implement them, you can compose I/O like Lego — and `bufio` wraps any Reader/Writer to batch syscalls for speed.

subtopics.title: io.Reader and io.Writer
subtopics.explanation: io.Reader has one method: Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) — fill p with up to len(p) bytes, return how many you wrote and any error. io.Writer has Write(p []byte) (n int, err error) — consume p, return how many bytes were written. These single-method interfaces are the universal currency of Go I/O: files, network connections, strings.Reader, bytes.Buffer all satisfy them. Every other piece of the io, bufio & Readers/Writers toolkit builds on these two contracts.

subtopics.title: The (n, err) contract
subtopics.explanation: Read may return 0 < n <= len(p) bytes AND a non-nil error in the same call. The correct pattern is: process the n bytes FIRST, then check the error. A Reader that returns data with io.EOF is valid; callers must not discard the n bytes just because err != nil. This contract is the foundation every Reader in the io, bufio & Readers/Writers world must honor.

subtopics.title: io.EOF and end of stream
subtopics.explanation: io.EOF is the sentinel error meaning 'no more data.' It is returned (eventually) by Read when the stream is exhausted — sometimes alongside the final bytes, sometimes on a final empty read. Treat io.EOF as a normal end condition, not a failure; check it with errors.Is(err, io.EOF) or == io.EOF. Recognizing io.EOF as success is what lets the io, bufio & Readers/Writers helpers stop cleanly rather than reporting a fake error.

subtopics.title: Composition with io.Copy & friends
subtopics.explanation: Because everything is a Reader/Writer, helpers compose: io.Copy(dst, src) streams src into dst with a small internal buffer; io.MultiWriter fans one write out to many; io.TeeReader reads while copying to a writer. You rarely hand-roll loops — you wire pipes together. This composability is the whole payoff of the io, bufio & Readers/Writers abstraction.

subtopics.title: bufio for batching
subtopics.explanation: Raw Read/Write often map to syscalls; doing them byte-by-byte is slow. bufio.NewReader and bufio.NewWriter add an in-memory buffer so many small operations become few large syscalls. bufio.Reader also adds ReadString, ReadLine, etc.; bufio.Writer requires a final Flush() to push buffered bytes out. Buffering and Flush are the performance layer of the io, bufio & Readers/Writers stack.

subtopics.title: bufio.Scanner for tokens
subtopics.explanation: bufio.Scanner is the easy way to read input token-by-token (lines by default, or words/runes via Split). It handles buffering and the EOF dance for you: loop while Scan() is true, read Text()/Bytes(), then check Err() once after the loop. Note its default max token size (64KB) — raise it with Buffer for long lines. Scanner is the ergonomic reading front-end of the io, bufio & Readers/Writers package.

foundations.overview: Go's I/O design is famously minimal: nearly all streaming I/O flows through io.Reader and io.Writer, each a single-method interface. This is what lets you write a function that takes an io.Reader and works equally on a file, a network socket, a string, or an HTTP request body — without knowing which. On top of these, the bufio package adds buffering (turning many tiny syscalls into a few big ones) and convenient line/token scanning. Mastering the Read contract, io.EOF handling, and when to wrap with bufio is core to writing correct and fast Go I/O.
foundations.formalDefinition: io.Reader is the interface { Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) } and io.Writer is { Write(p []byte) (n int, err error) }; together with their many implementations and the bufio buffering wrappers, they form Go's composable streaming-I/O abstraction.
foundations.whyItMatters: Almost every Go program does I/O — reading config, serving HTTP, copying files, parsing logs. Misunderstanding the (n, err) contract or io.EOF causes data loss and truncation bugs; missing a bufio.Flush silently drops output; not buffering hot paths wastes syscalls. These are common production and interview topics.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of Reader/Writer as standardized pipe fittings. Any source (file, socket, buffer) exposes the same outlet (Read); any sink exposes the same inlet (Write); so you can connect any source to any sink with io.Copy. bufio is a holding tank inserted in the pipe: it collects small trickles into one big flush, so the expensive valve (the syscall) opens rarely.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Each raw Read/Write on a file or socket typically crosses into the kernel via a syscall — relatively expensive. bufio amortizes that: a 4KB buffer turns 4096 one-byte writes into a single syscall. The Go runtime also integrates network Reads with the netpoller, parking the goroutine while the kernel waits, so blocking Reads don't waste a thread.
foundations.realWorldUsage: net/http request and response bodies are io.Readers/Writers; encoding/json decodes from a Reader; compress/gzip wraps a Reader/Writer; log files use bufio writers; parsers use bufio.Scanner. io.Copy underpins file servers and proxies.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct buffering dramatically cuts syscall and CPU overhead in I/O-heavy services (log shippers, proxies, file servers), lowering infrastructure cost; correct EOF/error handling prevents data-corruption incidents.
foundations.engineeringImpact: The single-method interfaces make I/O code highly testable (pass a bytes.Buffer or strings.Reader in tests) and composable. The risks are subtle: forgetting Flush, mishandling partial reads, or assuming one Read returns everything.
foundations.performanceImpact: Unbuffered byte-at-a-time I/O is syscall-bound and slow; bufio can be orders of magnitude faster. io.Copy uses an efficient internal buffer (and zero-copy fast paths like sendfile via ReaderFrom/WriterTo when available).
commonUseCases: Streaming an HTTP body with io.Copy
Wrapping streams: gzip, tee, multi-writer, limited reader
Testing I/O code with bytes.Buffer / strings.Reader

commonMisconceptions.myth: One Read fills the whole buffer.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Read may return fewer bytes than len(p) without error; you must loop, or use io.ReadFull / io.ReadAll when you need all of it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If Read returns an error, ignore any bytes it returned.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Read can return n > 0 AND a non-nil error (including io.EOF) in the same call — process the n bytes before checking err.

commonMisconceptions.myth: bufio.Writer flushes automatically when you're done.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You must call Flush() (or it stays buffered); forgetting Flush silently drops the tail of your output.

visualExplorer.caption: How a stream moves from a Reader to a Writer.

config.intro: io.Copy streams bytes without loading everything into memory:

steps.name: Allocate a buffer
steps.detail: io.Copy uses a small internal buffer (or a zero-copy fast path if src/dst support ReaderFrom/WriterTo).

steps.name: Read a chunk
steps.detail: It calls src.Read(buf), which fills up to len(buf) bytes and returns (n, err).

steps.name: Write what was read
steps.detail: It writes exactly buf[:n] to dst, retrying until all n bytes are written.

steps.name: Loop until EOF
steps.detail: It repeats read→write. When Read returns io.EOF, copying stops cleanly.

steps.name: Return total & error
steps.detail: It returns the total bytes copied and any non-EOF error; EOF is treated as success.

interactiveExamples.title: Same code, any source: counting bytes from a Reader
interactiveExamples.explanation: CountBytes takes an io.Reader, so it works on a string, a file, or a network body unchanged. Note the loop and the process-then-check-error pattern: bytes returned alongside io.EOF must still be counted.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: buffer writes and don't lose the tail
interactiveExamples.explanation: This writes 1000 lines to an io.Writer. As written it issues many small writes and may lose buffered data. Wrap the writer with bufio and ensure everything is flushed. Reveal the solution for the idiomatic defer-Flush pattern.

code.expectedOutput:
line 0
line 1
...
line 999
(1000 lines; batched into few syscalls)

checkpoints.prompt: This read loop sometimes drops the last few bytes. What's the bug?
options: It breaks on error before processing the n bytes that Read returned alongside io.EOF
process should take buf, not buf[:n]
checkpoints.explanation: Read may return n > 0 together with io.EOF on the final call. Breaking before processing buf[:n] discards those last bytes. Always process the n bytes first, then check the error — or use io.ReadAll/io.Copy which handle this for you.

checkpoints.code:
var b bytes.Buffer
w := bufio.NewWriter(&b)
fmt.Fprint(w, "hello")
fmt.Println(b.Len())
checkpoints.explanation: The bytes are still in the bufio.Writer's internal buffer; they haven't reached the underlying bytes.Buffer yet. b.Len() is 0 until you call w.Flush(). This is the classic 'forgot to Flush' trap.

checkpoints.prompt: You need to read an entire (reasonably small) io.Reader into a []byte. What's the idiomatic call?
options: A manual for loop calling Read
checkpoints.explanation: io.ReadAll(r) reads until EOF and returns all bytes, handling partial reads and the EOF dance for you. A single big Read isn't guaranteed to return everything, and the manual loops are unnecessary boilerplate for this case.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the line so the loop reads the input line by line.
checkpoints.explanation: bufio.Scanner advances with Scan(), which returns false at EOF or on error; you then read the token with Text()/Bytes() and check Err() once after the loop. Read/Next/HasNext aren't Scanner methods.

codeLab.title: Count non-empty lines from any Reader
codeLab.instructions: Implement `CountNonEmpty(r io.Reader) (int, error)` that returns how many lines in r are non-empty (a line is the text between newlines; trailing whitespace counts as content, but a fully empty line does not). Use bufio.Scanner and report any scan error.
hints: bufio.NewScanner defaults to splitting on lines, so each Scan() yields one line.
A 'non-empty' line is one where sc.Text() != "".
Scan() returns false on both EOF and error — always check sc.Err() after the loop.

debuggingLab.title: The file is missing its last lines
debuggingLab.symptom: A program writes thousands of lines to a file via a bufio.Writer, but the file on disk is truncated — the final chunk is missing.

brokenCode.caption: Data left in the bufio buffer never reaches the file.

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: bufio.Writer accumulates writes in memory and only sends them to the underlying file when its buffer fills OR when you call Flush(). Here the last partial buffer is never flushed, so those rows are lost. Closing the file does NOT flush the bufio buffer — bufio doesn't know about f.Close(). You must Flush the bufio.Writer explicitly, and before the file is closed.
commonMistakes: Assuming f.Close() flushes the bufio.Writer (it doesn't).
Deferring Close before Flush so they run in the wrong order.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Flush the bufio.Writer before the file is closed, and check the Flush error.

theory.question: Describe the io.Reader Read contract and the correct way to consume a Reader in a loop.
theory.directAnswer: Read(p []byte) returns (n, err): it fills up to len(p) bytes into p, returns n bytes actually read, and an error. Crucially, n can be > 0 even when err is non-nil (including io.EOF), and a single Read may return fewer than len(p) bytes without any error. The correct loop processes buf[:n] FIRST, then checks the error: break/return on io.EOF (treated as success), propagate other errors. Or sidestep it with io.ReadAll, io.ReadFull, or io.Copy.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The semantic contract every Reader implementation must honor.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To support streaming sources that deliver data incrementally and signal end-of-stream in the same call as the last bytes.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Callers loop, consuming the n returned bytes each iteration and stopping on io.EOF.

theory.whyImportant: Mishandling it causes truncation and data-loss bugs; it's a classic Go correctness probe.
theory.realWorldExample: Reading an HTTP response body: the network delivers data in chunks, so each Read returns a partial buffer until EOF.

followUps.question: When would you use io.ReadFull instead?
followUps.answer: When you need exactly len(buf) bytes and want an error (ErrUnexpectedEOF) if the stream ends early — e.g. reading a fixed-size header.

followUps.question: Is io.EOF an error you should log?
followUps.answer: No — it's the normal end-of-stream sentinel; treat it as success and stop reading.

theory.question: Why wrap a Reader/Writer with bufio, and what's the one thing you must not forget?
theory.directAnswer: bufio adds an in-memory buffer so many small reads/writes become a few large syscalls, which can be orders of magnitude faster on hot I/O paths; bufio.Reader also offers ReadString/ReadLine and bufio.Scanner offers token scanning. The thing you must not forget is bufio.Writer.Flush(): buffered bytes aren't written to the underlying destination until the buffer fills or you Flush, and closing the underlying file does NOT flush the bufio buffer.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A buffering layer over any Reader/Writer.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Raw Read/Write often map to syscalls; buffering amortizes that cost.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Writes accumulate until the buffer fills or Flush is called; reads pull a big chunk and serve it piecemeal.

theory.whyImportant: A forgotten Flush silently drops the tail of output — a common, hard-to-spot production bug.
theory.realWorldExample: A log writer wraps the file in bufio.NewWriter and defers Flush so thousands of log lines become a handful of syscalls.

followUps.question: Does bufio.Scanner need a Flush?
followUps.answer: No — Scanner is read-only; you just loop on Scan() and check Err() afterward. Flush is a Writer concern.

theory.question: Compare io.ReadAll, io.ReadFull, and io.Copy — when do you reach for each, and what are the memory implications?
theory.directAnswer: io.ReadAll(r) reads until EOF and returns every byte in a single []byte — convenient but it buffers the whole payload in memory, so only use it on bounded, small inputs. io.ReadFull(r, buf) reads EXACTLY len(buf) bytes or returns an error (io.ErrUnexpectedEOF if the stream ends early) — ideal for fixed-size headers or framed protocols. io.Copy(dst, src) streams from a Reader to a Writer through a small internal buffer, so peak memory is the buffer size, not the payload size — the right choice for large or unbounded data. The rule of thumb: ReadAll for small known-size blobs, ReadFull for exact-length frames, Copy for streaming anything large.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three stdlib helpers that consume a Reader with different completeness and memory profiles.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different tasks need different guarantees: 'all of it', 'exactly N bytes', or 'stream it through without buffering'.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: ReadAll grows a slice until EOF; ReadFull loops until len(buf) bytes arrive or the stream ends short; Copy loops read→write with a fixed buffer until EOF.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing ReadAll on a large payload is a classic OOM cause; knowing the three is a common correctness-and-scalability probe.
theory.realWorldExample: A file server uses io.Copy to stream multi-GB downloads; a binary protocol parser uses io.ReadFull to read a fixed 8-byte length prefix; a config loader uses io.ReadAll on a small file.

followUps.question: What error does io.ReadFull return if the stream ends early?
followUps.answer: io.ErrUnexpectedEOF if it read some but not all bytes, or io.EOF if it read zero bytes before the stream ended.

followUps.question: How do you bound io.ReadAll safely on untrusted input?
followUps.answer: Wrap the reader in io.LimitReader(r, max) (or http.MaxBytesReader) so ReadAll stops after max bytes instead of buffering an attacker-controlled amount.

theory.question: What are io.TeeReader and io.MultiWriter, and when would you compose them?
theory.directAnswer: io.TeeReader(r, w) returns a Reader that, as bytes are read from r, also writes them to w — so you can observe or mirror a stream while a downstream consumer reads it, in a single pass. io.MultiWriter(w1, w2, ...) returns a Writer that fans every write out to all the given writers. You compose them when you need to process a stream and simultaneously capture it: e.g. TeeReader to feed a hash while uploading, or MultiWriter to write a response to both the network and a log at once. Both are pure composition over the Reader/Writer interfaces — no extra passes over the data.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Composition helpers that split or mirror a stream without re-reading it.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To do side-work (hashing, logging, checksumming) inline with the main copy, avoiding a second full pass over the bytes.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: TeeReader writes each chunk it reads to its writer before returning it; MultiWriter's Write calls each underlying writer in turn, failing on the first error.

theory.whyImportant: Single-pass tee/fan-out is the idiomatic way to add checksums, mirroring, and auditing to I/O paths — a favorite composition question.
theory.realWorldExample: An upload handler wraps the body in io.TeeReader(body, sha256Hasher) so it computes the content hash while streaming the bytes to object storage in one pass.

followUps.question: What happens if one MultiWriter target returns an error?
followUps.answer: Write stops and returns that error immediately; the remaining writers do not receive the chunk, so treat MultiWriter as all-or-nothing per write.

followUps.question: Does TeeReader buffer the whole stream?
followUps.answer: No — it mirrors each chunk as it's read, so memory stays bounded by the caller's read buffer size.

scenario.question: A service proxies large file uploads from a client to object storage and is OOMing under load. The code does io.ReadAll on the request body then uploads the bytes. How do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: io.ReadAll buffers the entire body in memory, so concurrent large uploads exhaust RAM. Stream instead: pass the request body (an io.Reader) directly to the storage client's upload, or use io.Copy to pipe body → storage writer with a small fixed buffer. This keeps memory bounded regardless of file size. Add an io.LimitReader to cap maximum upload size and protect against abuse.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Reader/Writer interfaces let you move bytes without materializing the whole payload.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: io.Copy reads a chunk and writes it, looping until EOF, so peak memory is the buffer size, not the file size.

scenario.whyImportant: Buffering whole payloads is a frequent cause of OOMs in proxies and upload handlers.
scenario.realWorldExample: An upload handler does io.Copy(s3PartWriter, io.LimitReader(r.Body, maxBytes)) and stays flat on memory under heavy load.

followUps.question: How do you cap the upload size safely?
followUps.answer: Wrap the body in io.LimitReader(r.Body, max) (or http.MaxBytesReader), so reads stop after max bytes and the handler can reject oversized uploads.

scenario.question: A log-processing job reads a huge file with bufio.Scanner and crashes with 'bufio.Scanner: token too long' on certain inputs. What's happening and how do you fix it robustly?
scenario.directAnswer: bufio.Scanner has a default maximum token size of 64KB (bufio.MaxScanTokenSize). A single line longer than that overflows the internal buffer and Scan() returns false with bufio.ErrTooLong from Err(). The quick fix is sc.Buffer(make([]byte, 0, initial), maxBytes) to raise the cap — but sizing maxBytes to a bounded value is important so a pathological or malicious line can't exhaust memory. For truly unbounded lines you shouldn't use Scanner at all; switch to bufio.Reader.ReadString('\n') or ReadLine, which stream partial lines instead of requiring the whole token to fit in one buffer.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A token-length limit in Scanner colliding with abnormally long lines.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Scanner deliberately bounds its buffer to prevent a single huge token from causing unbounded allocation.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When a token exceeds the buffer and the buffer is already at its max, Scan returns false and Err reports bufio.ErrTooLong.

scenario.whyImportant: It's a common surprise in log/CSV/NDJSON processing and tests judgment about bounding untrusted input.
scenario.realWorldExample: A pipeline ingesting user-generated JSON lines hit ErrTooLong on a 200KB record; the team raised Scanner's buffer to a bounded 1MB and rejected anything larger as malformed.

followUps.question: Why not just set the buffer arbitrarily large?
followUps.answer: An unbounded max lets one giant line allocate huge memory, turning malformed input into a DoS; pick a deliberate ceiling and reject beyond it.

followUps.question: When is bufio.Reader.ReadString better than Scanner?
followUps.answer: When lines can be arbitrarily long and you must stream them, since ReadString/ReadLine hand back partial data instead of needing the whole token buffered.

systemDesign.question: Design a streaming file-transformation service: it accepts an uploaded file, gzip-compresses it, computes a SHA-256 checksum, and writes the result to object storage — all without buffering the whole file in memory. How do you wire the io.Reader/io.Writer stack?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Build a Reader/Writer pipeline so bytes flow through once with bounded memory. On the request side, wrap the body in http.MaxBytesReader (or io.LimitReader) to cap size. Then compose the write side: create a gzip.Writer that targets an io.MultiWriter fanning out to (a) the object-storage upload writer and (b) a sha256 hasher. io.Copy(gzipWriter, limitedBody) streams the upload → gzip → {storage, hash} in one pass; peak memory is just the small copy buffer plus gzip's window. After the copy, Close the gzip.Writer (to flush its trailer), read the checksum from the hasher, and finalize the storage upload. Set context deadlines so a stalled client or storage backend can't pin the goroutine, and check every Write/Close error.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A single-pass, bounded-memory transform built purely from composed Reader/Writer wrappers.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Files can be arbitrarily large, so materializing them in memory doesn't scale; composition lets each byte flow through compression, hashing, and storage exactly once.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: gzip.Writer sits over an io.MultiWriter{storage, hasher}; io.Copy pumps the limited body into gzip, which fans compressed bytes to both sinks; closing gzip flushes the final block.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It exercises the whole io/bufio toolkit — LimitReader, MultiWriter, io.Copy, streaming compression, Close/flush semantics — the way real upload/ETL services are built.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A backup service streams client uploads through gzip and a hasher into S3 with io.Copy, keeping memory flat regardless of file size and recording the checksum for integrity verification.

followUps.question: Why must you Close the gzip.Writer before finalizing the upload?
followUps.answer: gzip buffers and only writes its final block and trailer on Close; skipping it produces a truncated, corrupt archive — analogous to forgetting bufio.Flush.

followUps.question: Where would bufio fit into this pipeline?
followUps.answer: Wrap the storage writer in a bufio.Writer if the storage client issues many tiny syscalls, batching them; remember to Flush it before Close.

followUps.question: How do you bound memory against a malicious huge upload?
followUps.answer: http.MaxBytesReader / io.LimitReader caps the total bytes read, so the streaming pipeline (already O(1) memory) also rejects oversized inputs instead of processing them.

coding.question: Implement `CopyN(dst io.Writer, src io.Reader, n int64) (int64, error)` that copies at most n bytes from src to dst, returning the number copied. Do it with composition, not a hand-rolled loop.
coding.thoughtProcess: Copying 'at most n bytes from a Reader to a Writer' is exactly io.LimitReader + io.Copy. LimitReader(src, n) yields a Reader that reports EOF after n bytes; io.Copy then streams it to dst with bounded memory and handles the partial-read/EOF contract for me. (This mirrors what the stdlib's io.CopyN does.)
coding.lineByLine: io.LimitReader(src, n) returns a Reader that delivers at most n bytes, then reports io.EOF. io.Copy reads from that limited reader and writes to dst in a loop using a small internal buffer, returning the total bytes written. io.Copy already implements the process-then-check-error contract and treats EOF as a clean stop, so we just return its result.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — io.Copy uses a small fixed buffer; no full-payload buffering.

followUps.question: How does this differ from the stdlib io.CopyN?
followUps.answer: It's essentially the same implementation; the real io.CopyN also returns io.EOF if fewer than n bytes were available, signaling the source was shorter than requested.

followUps.question: Why is composition preferred over a manual read/write loop?
followUps.answer: io.Copy already handles partial reads, short writes, and EOF correctly; reusing it avoids re-introducing those subtle bugs.

coding.question: Implement `func CountingReader(r io.Reader) (io.Reader, *int64)` that wraps r and returns a Reader plus a pointer whose value tracks how many bytes have been read so far. It must honor the Read contract.
coding.thoughtProcess: I need a wrapper type embedding/holding the underlying Reader and a byte counter. Its Read delegates to the inner Read, then adds the returned n to the counter BEFORE returning — respecting that n can be > 0 even alongside io.EOF. I return a pointer to the counter so the caller can observe progress. Using atomic isn't strictly required if a single goroutine reads, but I'll keep it simple and correct for the single-reader contract (a Reader isn't safe for concurrent use anyway).
coding.lineByLine: countingReader holds the wrapped Reader and a pointer to the counter. Its Read calls the inner Read, then adds the returned n to *c.n before returning — this ordering is critical because Read may return n > 0 together with io.EOF, and dropping those bytes would undercount. CountingReader allocates the counter, hands back the wrapper and the pointer, so the caller sees the total grow as it reads (e.g. after io.Copy or io.ReadAll completes).
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) overhead per Read call; O(total bytes) overall — same as the underlying reader.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — one wrapper struct and one int64 counter, no buffering.

followUps.question: How would you make this safe for concurrent reads?
followUps.answer: Use atomic.AddInt64/atomic.LoadInt64 on the counter — though note a single io.Reader is generally not safe for concurrent Read calls, so the counter is usually the lesser concern.

followUps.question: How does this compare to io.TeeReader?
followUps.answer: TeeReader mirrors bytes to a Writer; this only counts them. You could implement counting by teeing into a writer that just tallies len(p), but a direct wrapper is cheaper.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Design APIs around io.Reader/io.Writer rather than concrete types so callers can plug in files, sockets, buffers, or test fakes. Compose with io.Copy, io.MultiWriter, io.TeeReader, and io.LimitReader instead of hand-rolling byte loops.
productionDeepDive.performance: Wrap hot raw streams with bufio to batch syscalls; prefer streaming (io.Copy) over io.ReadAll for large payloads to keep memory bounded. Reuse buffers with sync.Pool in very high-throughput paths, and rely on ReaderFrom/WriterTo fast paths (e.g. sendfile) that io.Copy exploits automatically.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: A single Reader/Writer is generally not safe for concurrent use; give each goroutine its own, or synchronize. io.Pipe connects a writer goroutine to a reader goroutine safely for streaming hand-offs.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Always check and propagate Read/Write errors, treat io.EOF as a normal stop, and ensure bufio.Writer.Flush runs (and its error is checked) before the underlying resource closes. Set deadlines on network conns so a stalled peer can't block a Read forever.
productionDeepDive.observability: Wrap streams with a counting/teeing Reader to record bytes transferred and feed metrics; io.TeeReader can mirror a stream to a hash or log without an extra pass.
productionDeepDive.security: Bound untrusted input with io.LimitReader / http.MaxBytesReader to prevent memory-exhaustion DoS, and raise bufio.Scanner's buffer deliberately rather than reading unbounded lines.

caseStudies.problem: Move large request/response bodies without buffering them in memory.
caseStudies.solution: Stream with io.Copy between Readers and Writers, leveraging sendfile fast paths.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Streaming complicates retries (the body is consumed once) but keeps memory flat.
caseStudies.lessons: Treat bodies as streams; never io.ReadAll arbitrary-size payloads.

caseStudies.solution: Wrap outputs in bufio.Writer and flush periodically; parse inputs with bufio.Scanner.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Buffering adds a flush-on-shutdown requirement and slight latency.
caseStudies.lessons: Buffering turns many tiny syscalls into a few large ones — a large, cheap win.

keyTakeaways: io.Reader (Read) and io.Writer (Write) are single-method interfaces that nearly all Go I/O implements, making streams composable across files, sockets, and buffers.
Honor the Read contract: process the n returned bytes before checking err, treat io.EOF as a normal end, and don't assume one Read fills the buffer.
Compose instead of looping — io.Copy, io.LimitReader, io.MultiWriter, io.TeeReader — and stream large payloads rather than io.ReadAll-ing them.
Wrap hot streams with bufio to batch syscalls, and always Flush() a bufio.Writer (before closing the underlying file) or you'll silently lose the tail.
